procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a trial court or police station where FIR No. 35/2015 was registered.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 28.03.2016 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Nagpur Bench at Nagpur allowing Criminal Application No.380 of 2015, thereby quashing FIR No. 35/2015.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The first respondent (Vinayak Deorao Bhagat) filed Criminal Application No. 380 of 2015 in the High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. seeking to quash FIR No. 35/2015, which was registered based on a report by the appellant (Narayan Malhari Thorat). The High Court granted the application and quashed the FIR.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (Narayan Malhari Thorat) appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court's decision to quash the FIR. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and directed the concerned authorities to complete the investigation into the matter.

directions: The judgment and order under appeal is set aside.
The concerned authorities to complete the investigation as early as possible.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing an FIR for an offense under Section 306 IPC by examining the prima facie evidence and the accused's intention, in the exercise of its jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C.

facts: The appellant's son committed suicide, leaving a suicide note that made a definite allegation against the first respondent.
An FIR was registered against the respondent for abetment of suicide under Section 306 IPC.
The allegations were that the respondent, a colleague of the victim's wife, would constantly call and harass her.
The victim had confronted the respondent about this, leading to an altercation 3-4 days before the suicide.
The respondent filed a petition in the High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash the FIR.
The High Court quashed the FIR before the police investigation was completed.
law: The jurisdiction of a High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash an FIR should be exercised sparingly.

At a preliminary stage, when an investigation is not yet complete and no charge-sheet has been filed, the High Court should not delve into a detailed examination of the evidence to determine factual questions, such as the accused's intention or mental element (mens rea).
application: The Supreme Court observed that there were specific and definite allegations against the respondent, supported by the suicide note and statements from the victim's wife and mother.
It noted that an altercation had taken place between the victim and the respondent shortly before the suicide.
The Court reasoned that in light of these facts, and because the investigation was still ongoing, the High Court acted improperly.

It was premature for the High Court to analyze the prima facie evidence to decide whether the respondent had the requisite intention to aid, instigate, or abet the suicide. This question, the Court held, should be left for the investigation to uncover.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in quashing the FIR by examining the respondent's intention at a stage when the investigation was incomplete. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and directed the authorities to complete the investigation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing an FIR for an offense under Section 306 IPC by examining the prima facie evidence and the accused's intention, in the exercise of its jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was not justified in quashing the FIR by examining whether the record prima facie established that the respondent had the requisite intention for an offense under Section 306 IPC, as this was an overreach of its jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C.
respondent_arguments: The respondent, relying on previous Supreme Court decisions (Netai Dutta v. State of W.B. and M. Mohan v. State), argued that the High Court was correct to examine the evidence, such as the suicide note, to determine if a prima facie case of abetment was made out before allowing the proceedings to continue.

cases.case_name: M. Mohan v. State represented by the Deputy Superintendent of Police
cases.principle: To sustain a charge under Section 306 IPC, the material on record must establish that the accused is at least remotely connected with the offence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A High Court is not justified in quashing a First Information Report under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by entering into a detailed examination of whether the record prima facie establishes the requisite intention for an offense under Section 306 of the Indian Penal Code, as such questions are to be determined during the investigation and trial.
obiter: The court has not expressed any opinion on the merits of the matter, which shall be considered at the appropriate stage.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Given that there were definite allegations against the respondent—supported by witness statements, a recent altercation, and a suicide note—the High Court was not justified in using its Section 482 Cr.P.C. jurisdiction to quash the FIR by delving into the question of whether the respondent had the requisite intention or mental element to abet suicide. Such an inquiry is premature when the investigation is not yet complete and a charge-sheet has not been filed.
legal_tests_applied: Whether, at the initial stage of an investigation, the allegations in the FIR and materials collected prima facie disclose the commission of an offense that requires further investigation, without conducting a detailed examination into the accused's mental element or intention.
why_respondent_won: The High Court overstepped its jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C. by prematurely entering into the question of the accused's intention.
There were definite allegations that the respondent harassed the victim's wife, supported by statements from the victim's mother and wife.
An altercation had occurred between the victim and the respondent 3-4 days prior to the suicide.
The suicide note contained a definite allegation against the respondent.

At a stage where the investigation was incomplete and no charge-sheet was filed, the High Court ought not to have gone into the aspect of whether there was the requisite mental element or intention on the part of the respondent.
policy_considerations: The High Court's power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. should not be used to stall a criminal investigation at a nascent stage by conducting a mini-trial on aspects like intent, especially when there are specific allegations and evidence that warrant a full investigation by the proper authorities.
